meta.status: Drafted by AI from the cited university extension sources. Every entry needs review by an agriculture expert before it is relied on in the field (needs_review: true).
meta.content_rules: Cultural practices, plus generic treatment categories (for example 'a fungicide labelled for this disease') that always send the farmer to the extension officer and the product label. Never product or active-ingredient names, doses, spray intervals or application methods.
meta.extension_fallback: Consult your local agriculture extension officer for approved products and doses.
meta.disclaimer: General guidance only, not a diagnosis. Please consult an agriculture expert.

risk_levels.meaning: General potential of the disease to cause crop loss (from the cited extension sources), NOT measured from the photo.
risk_levels.low: Usually limited damage if basic care is followed.
risk_levels.medium: Can reduce yield or quality if ignored; act within days.
risk_levels.high: Can cause heavy losses quickly; act immediately and contact an expert.

diseases.description: A fungal disease that causes olive-green to dark, velvety spots on leaves and scabby, cracked spots on fruit.
symptoms: Olive-green to brown, velvety spots on leaves
Spots darken; badly affected leaves yellow and drop early
Dark, corky, sometimes cracked scabs on fruit
diseases.spread: The fungus overwinters in fallen infected leaves. In spring, rain and wind carry spores to new leaves and fruit during wet weather.
general_management: Rake up fallen leaves in autumn and destroy or thoroughly compost them
Prune to open the canopy so leaves dry quickly
Remove suckers and crowded interior shoots
Plant scab-resistant varieties where possible
Avoid overhead watering
diseases.risk_reason: Rarely kills trees, but in wet springs it can spoil much of the fruit and make leaves drop early.
causes: Fungus (Venturia inaequalis) that survives in fallen infected leaves
Cool, wet spring weather that keeps leaves wet for many hours
immediate_actions: Pick off badly spotted leaves and fruit and remove them from the orchard
Collect fallen leaves under the tree so they cannot infect new growth
Keep leaves dry: do not water over the canopy
treatment_categories: Fungicide labelled for this disease on this crop, started early (it protects new growth but does not heal spots) — ask your agriculture extension officer which product is approved locally, and follow the label exactly
call_expert_when: Spots spread quickly to new leaves or neighbouring plants
You are not sure which problem it is
Many fruits show scabs or cracks

diseases.description: A fungal disease that causes 'frog-eye' leaf spots, a firm black fruit rot and cankers on branches.
symptoms: Small purple leaf spots that turn brown in the centre with a purple edge (frog-eye)
Fruit rot that usually starts at the blossom end and turns brown to black

diseases.spread: Spores come from mummified fruit, dead wood and cankers and are spread by rain splash. The fungus can live on many trees and shrubs, so spores are common.
general_management: Remove mummified fruit from trees and from the ground
Prune out dead wood and cankered branches in the dormant season and destroy them
Clean up prunings and fallen fruit around the trees
Keep trees vigorous with good pruning and balanced nutrition
diseases.risk_reason: Causes fruit rot and branch cankers; losses grow when mummified fruit and dead wood stay in the orchard.
causes: Fungus (Botryosphaeria obtusa) living in dead wood, cankers and mummified fruit
Rain splash, wounds and stressed trees
immediate_actions: Remove rotten and mummified fruit from the tree and the ground
Cut out dead or cankered branches and take them away from the orchard
Clean pruning tools after cutting diseased wood
treatment_categories: Fungicide labelled for this disease on this crop, started early (it protects new growth but does not heal spots) — ask your agriculture extension officer which product is approved locally, and follow the label exactly
call_expert_when: Spots spread quickly to new leaves or neighbouring plants

Branches show sunken cankers or die back

diseases.description: A fungal disease that needs both apple and juniper (cedar) trees; it causes bright orange-yellow spots on apple leaves.

general_management: Plant rust-resistant apple varieties
Where practical, remove nearby junipers/red cedars or the galls on them
Inspect junipers in late winter and prune off galls before spring rains
Watch apple leaves closely after wet spring weather
diseases.risk_reason: Usually weakens leaves and spots fruit; serious mainly where junipers grow close to susceptible apple varieties.
causes: Fungus that needs both juniper (cedar) and apple trees
Spring rains that release spores from galls on nearby junipers
immediate_actions: Look for orange, jelly-like galls on nearby juniper/cedar trees and cut them off
Remove badly spotted leaves
Note the variety: plan resistant varieties for new planting

Remove confirmed infected trees as advised by local authorities

treatment_categories: No cure. Psyllid control and removal of confirmed infected trees are coordinated by the agriculture department — do not treat on your own
